headings.title: Introduction to Safe Delivery and the Clean Birth Kit
headings.content: Safe delivery is a critical component of maternal and child health nursing, aiming to achieve optimal health outcomes for both the mother and the newborn while minimizing morbidity and mortality. In many resource-constrained settings across Nigeria, preventable infections and complications during childbirth remain major public health concerns. A fundamental intervention promoted by the World Health Organization and adopted in Nigerian primary healthcare systems is the use of the clean birth kit. This kit typically contains simple, essential items such as a clean plastic sheet to provide a clean surface for delivery, soap for washing the mother's perineum, a new or sterile blade for cutting the umbilical cord, a clean tie or clamp for the cord, and a clean cloth for drying the baby. Nursing students must understand that utilizing a clean birth kit significantly reduces the incidence of neonatal tetanus and puerperal sepsis, which are leading causes of maternal and neonatal mortality in developing regions. Nurses play a pivotal role not only in utilizing these items correctly during hospital and community births but also in educating traditional birth attendants and pregnant women on the importance of cleanliness and hygiene during labor and delivery. By mastering the components and rationale of the clean birth kit, student nurses contribute directly to the global sustainable development goals targeting the reduction of maternal and neonatal mortality rates.

headings.title: Preparation of the Delivery Environment and Equipment
headings.content: Preparing the delivery environment and equipment is a foundational competency for student nurses working in maternity units. A well-prepared delivery room ensures readiness for normal physiological childbirth as well as unexpected obstetric emergencies. The environment must be warm, well-lit, draft-free, and private to promote the parturient's comfort and psychological well-being. Equipment preparation involves assembling, checking, and sterilely arranging all necessary instruments before the expected time of birth. Essential equipment includes delivery trays containing forceps, needle holders, suture materials, scissors, artery forceps, kidney dishes, and sterile gauze swabs. Additionally, resuscitation equipment for both mother and baby must be fully checked and functional, including oxygen sources, suction apparatus, bags, and masks of appropriate sizes. In Nigerian clinical settings, ensuring that emergency drugs such as oxytocin, ergometrine, and magnesium sulfate are readily available and unexpired is a critical safety measure. Nursing students must practice aseptic techniques diligently while setting up tables, ensuring that sterile barriers are not breached and contaminated items are immediately discarded. Proper preparation minimizes delays during critical moments of delivery, directly enhancing clinical outcomes and patient safety.

headings.title: Monitoring and Assessment During the First and Second Stages of Labour
headings.content: Monitoring and assessment during the first and second stages of labor require vigilance, clinical acumen, and empathy from the nurse. During the first stage of labor, which spans from the onset of true labor pains to full cervical dilation, the nurse monitors uterine contractions for frequency, duration, and intensity, alongside continuous or intermittent assessment of fetal well-being. The partograph is an essential graphical tool used in Nigerian hospitals to record maternal and fetal parameters, including cervical dilation, descent of the fetal head, maternal pulse, blood pressure, and urine output, helping to identify prolonged labor early. Vaginal examinations are performed using strict aseptic techniques to assess cervical change and membrane status, though frequency should be limited to prevent infection. As the labor transitions into the second stage—from full dilation to the birth of the baby—the nurse supports the mother's urge to push, monitors maternal vital signs closely, and continuously tracks the fetal heart rate before and immediately after contractions. Recognizing signs of fetal distress, such as meconium-stained liquor or abnormal fetal heart rate patterns, allows the nurse to intervene promptly or escalate care to senior medical personnel. Effective communication reassures the parturient, reducing anxiety and promoting a positive birth experience.

headings.title: The Clean Delivery Process: The Essential Cleans
headings.content: The clean delivery process is governed by the practice of the essential cleans, which are vital interventions designed to prevent healthcare-associated and community-acquired infections during childbirth. These core principles include ensuring clean hands, a clean delivery surface, clean perineum, clean cord cutting, and clean cord care. First, healthcare providers must perform thorough hand hygiene using soap and water or alcohol-based hand rubs, followed by donning sterile gloves. Second, the delivery surface must be clean and sanitized, utilizing sterile drapes or clean plastic sheets to prevent contamination from beddings. Third, the mother's perineum and vulva must be washed with an appropriate antiseptic solution from front to back to reduce the bacterial load entering the birth canal. Fourth, the umbilical cord must be cut using a sterile or autoclaved instrument to prevent tetanus and sepsis. Finally, clean cord care involves keeping the cord stump clean and dry, avoiding the application of harmful traditional substances such as saliva, ash, or cow dung, which are documented risk factors for neonatal sepsis and omphalitis in local Nigerian communities. Student nurses must champion these practices through health education for mothers and families.

headings.title: Immediate Care of the Newborn and Apgar Scoring
headings.content: Immediate care of the newborn begins the moment the baby is delivered, focusing on establishing and maintaining adequate respiratory function and preventing hypothermia. As soon as the baby is born, the nurse notes the time of birth and gently dries the infant with a warm, clean towel, which simultaneously stimulates breathing and removes amniotic fluid to prevent heat loss through evaporation. Immediate assessment involves evaluating the newborn's cry, muscle tone, and breathing effort. The Apgar score is assessed at 1 minute and 5 minutes after birth, evaluating five distinct physiological parameters: Appearance (skin color), Pulse rate, Grimace (reflex irritability), Activity (muscle tone), and Respiration (respiratory effort). Each parameter is scored from 0 to 2, providing a total score out of 10 that guides the necessity of resuscitation or routine care. Routine immediate care also includes securing the airway if necessary, promoting early skin-to-skin contact on the mother's chest, initiating early breastfeeding within the first hour of life, and administering prophylactic eye care and vitamin K injection to prevent hemorrhagic disease of the newborn. Student nurses must perform these duties swiftly and methodically while maintaining a calm and reassuring presence for the parents.

headings.title: Management of the Third Stage of Labour and Prevention of PPH
headings.content: The third stage of labor spans from the birth of the baby until the complete expulsion of the placenta and fetal membranes. This phase carries the highest risk for postpartum hemorrhage (PPH), which remains a leading cause of maternal mortality in Nigeria. Active management of the third stage of labor (AMTSL) is the evidence-based standard of care recommended to prevent PPH. AMTSL consists of three core components: first, the administration of a uterotonic drug (preferably oxytocin 10 IU intramuscularly) within one minute of the baby's birth to stimulate uterine contractions; second, controlled cord traction combined with counter-pressure on the uterus (suprapubic sign) to deliver the placenta safely; and third, massage of the uterus through the maternal abdominal wall immediately after the placenta is delivered, followed by continued palpation to ensure the uterus remains contracted. The nurse must inspect the delivered placenta and membranes meticulously to ensure completeness, as retained placental fragments can cause delayed PPH and severe uterine infection. Monitoring vaginal bleeding, maternal vital signs, and uterine tone every 15 minutes during the immediate post-delivery period is mandatory for early detection of atony or lacerations.

headings.title: Infection Prevention and Control in Obstetric Practice
headings.content: Infection prevention and control (IPC) in obstetric practice is paramount to safeguarding both mother and neonate from healthcare-associated infections. Childbirth involves exposure to blood, amniotic fluid, and other potentially infectious body fluids, placing both healthcare providers and patients at risk of blood-borne pathogens such as HIV and Hepatitis B, as well as bacterial pathogens causing sepsis. Standard precautions must be observed at all times, including rigorous hand hygiene before and after patient contact, wearing appropriate personal protective equipment (PPE) such as sterile or examination gloves, aprons, face masks, and protective eyewear during delivery. Safe handling and disposal of sharp instruments—such as needles, blades, and suture needles—in puncture-resistant safety boxes are critical to prevent needle-stick injuries. Furthermore, all reusable instruments must undergo thorough decontamination, cleaning, and sterilization or high-level disinfection according to hospital protocols. Environmental hygiene, including the proper cleaning and disinfection of delivery beds, floors, and surfaces between patients, further curtails the transmission of hospital-acquired pathogens. Student nurses must internalize IPC protocols as a daily professional habit to promote a culture of safety in Nigerian healthcare institutions.

headings.title: Identification and Emergency Management of Intrapartum Complications
headings.content: Intrapartum complications can arise unexpectedly during labor, threatening the life and health of the mother and baby. Student nurses must be adept at identifying early warning signs and initiating emergency management. Common intrapartum complications include postpartum hemorrhage, shoulder dystocia, cord prolapse, uterine rupture, and fetal distress. For instance, shoulder dystocia—where the baby's shoulder becomes impacted behind the symphysis pubis—requires immediate implementation of maneuvers such as the McRoberts maneuver (hyperflexing the mother's legs against her abdomen) and suprapubic pressure, while avoiding fundal pressure. Cord prolapse, characterized by the umbilical cord descending ahead of the fetal presenting part, requires immediate relief of pressure on the cord by pushing the presenting part upward through a gloved vaginal examination, placing the mother in a knee-chest or exaggerated Sims position, and preparing for emergency Caesarean section. Fetal distress calls for stopping oxytocin infusions if running, changing the mother's position to lateral, administering supplemental oxygen, and notifying the obstetric team immediately. Prompt recognition, effective teamwork, clear communication using standardized protocols like SBAR, and decisive action are essential nursing competencies for managing these obstetric emergencies successfully.

headings.title: Postnatal Maternal Care and Documentation
headings.content: Postnatal maternal care and documentation complete the continuum of the safe delivery process, ensuring that the mother recovers safely from childbirth. Immediately following delivery, the mother remains in the recovery area for at least two hours. During this period, the nurse monitors vital signs, uterine involution (firmness of the uterus), vaginal bleeding amount, and bladder distension every 15 minutes for the first hour and every 30 minutes for the second hour. Encouraging early maternal voiding is crucial, as a full bladder can displace the uterus and lead to uterine atony and hemorrhage. Pain management for perineal lacerations or episiotomy sites, early ambulation, and nutritional counseling are also initiated. Documentation is a legal and clinical responsibility that must be accurate, comprehensive, and contemporaneous. The nurse must record the time of delivery, the condition of the mother and newborn, Apgar scores, estimated blood loss, medications administered, and any complications encountered or interventions performed. Detailed documentation protects the patient, guides subsequent nursing care plans, provides statistical data for healthcare facilities, and ensures continuity of care as the mother and baby transition to the postnatal ward.
